Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions and deconfined criticality in SrCu2(BO3)2

Yasir Iqbal Email: yiqbal@physics.iitm.ac.in Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India
Abstract

SrCu2(BO3)2 is the leading candidate for deconfined criticality, yet theories of its critical regime omit the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) interactions, which gap the kagome Dirac spin liquid. Adding them to the SU(2) gauge theory, we show that time reversal and a spin–orbit-locked glide forbid any gauge-singlet spinon mass to all orders. In-plane DM only twists the spinons, reconstructing the nodes below 0.030.03–0.170.17 K, while out-of-plane DM is irrelevant and SO(5) anisotropy arises only at second order. The material thus remains a platform for deconfined criticality, which NMR can test, since a [100][100] field induces a Néel moment and a [001][001] field does not.

SrCu2(BO3)2, a Shastry–Sutherland (SS) antiferromagnet [45, 22, 35, 36], is the most studied material candidate [25] for deconfined quantum criticality [43, 42]. Under pressure its plaquette-singlet phase gives way to an antiferromagnet [58, 14, 24], and whether a deconfined critical point controls that transition is debated. Field-tuned 11B NMR finds first-order signatures that weaken with pressure and suggests a proximate, likely multicritical, deconfined critical point, with quantum-critical scaling at 2.42.4 GPa near the transition field Hc≃5.7H_{c}\simeq 5.7 T [8]. Zero-field calorimetry finds a first-order transition with a bicritical point [15]. In applied fields near the critical pressure a TT-linear specific heat of open origin appears, possibly from fractionalized spin excitations [16, 47]. Between the SS model’s plaquette and Néel phases, numerical studies find a narrow gapless spin-liquid phase [57, 52, 6] (a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Dirac spin liquid [28]), a weakly first-order transition [56, 39], or a continuous one with emergent symmetry [26, 25]. On the theory side, an SU(2) gauge theory of Dirac fermions and adjoint Higgs fields, introduced for the square lattice [44], unifies the SS Dirac spin liquids with the Néel and valence-bond orders and supports an SO(5)-symmetric pseudocritical regime [11, 28, 29].

These field theories retain the SU(2) spin symmetry. The material, however, has Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) couplings of up to a few tenths of a meV [4, 23, 30, 41]. These have so far been included only in the dimer phase, at the dimer–plaquette transition [24] and in spin-wave analyses of the Néel phase [12, 2], and their absence from the theory of the deconfined scenario has been noted [7]. On the kagome lattice DM destabilizes the Dirac spin liquid: the out-of-plane DM component couples linearly to a time-reversal-even spin-triplet fermion mass of quantum-spin-Hall type, the hexagon vector chirality. It is relevant and was argued to drive magnetic order [18], as found numerically above D≃0.1​JD\simeq 0.1J [3] and in variational studies [17, 10]. The DM-driven transition has also been analyzed as one out of a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid of bosonic spinons [20]. Whether spin–orbit coupling can similarly gap the SS Dirac spin liquid, or otherwise destroy its criticality, has not been addressed.

Here, we answer this question by classifying the fermion bilinears of the continuum theory under the spin–orbit-locked symmetry group, in which every lattice operation also rotates the spins as an axial vector. We obtain the following results, summarized in Figs. 1 and 2. (i) Time reversal and a single locked glide forbid all six gauge-singlet fermion masses. (ii) Among the gauge-singlet bilinears, the in-plane DM couplings enter the critical theory only as a conserved spin current, with dimension exactly 2 and renormalization-group eigenvalue exactly 1 at a spin-rotation-invariant fixed point. Below the resulting scale T∗T^{*}, near the critical point and in a two-dimensional sample, the Dirac cones reconstruct into a quadratic band touching that, among gauge-singlet orders, only valence-bond or chirality order can gap. (iii) The largest inter-dimer coupling, the out-of-plane D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp}, induces no fermion bilinear without gradients and, with one gradient, only a spin-2 operator of dimension above 3 at any unitary critical point. At second order DM induces an SO(5)-breaking tensor whose relevance is disputed. (iv) A field along [100][100] induces a staggered Néel moment perpendicular to it, a field along [110][110] one along the field, and a field along [001][001] none.

Model and locked symmetry.—We study

H=J​∑dimers𝑺i⋅𝑺j+J′​∑squares𝑺i⋅𝑺j+∑⟨i​j⟩𝑫i​j⋅(𝑺i×𝑺j),H=J\!\sum_{\rm dimers}\!\bm{S}_{i}\!\cdot\!\bm{S}_{j}+J^{\prime}\!\sum_{\rm squares}\!\bm{S}_{i}\!\cdot\!\bm{S}_{j}+\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\bm{D}_{ij}\!\cdot\!(\bm{S}_{i}\times\bm{S}_{j}), (1)

with the DM vectors allowed by the crystal structure. Above Ts≃395T_{s}\simeq 395 K the space group is I​4/m​c​mI4/mcm and only the alternating out-of-plane inter-dimer component D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} is allowed [48, 4]; below TsT_{s} the buckling of the CuBO3 layers (I​4¯​2​mI\bar{4}2m, tetragonal up to the monoclinic onset at 44–55 GPa [27, 59]) adds an in-plane intra-dimer DD and two in-plane inter-dimer components D′∥,sD^{\prime}_{\parallel,s}, D′∥,nsD^{\prime}_{\parallel,ns} [48, 23, 5, 41]. With DM the spins can no longer be rotated independently of the lattice. A lattice operation OO acts on a spin as the axial vector 𝑺→det(O)​O​𝑺\bm{S}\to\det(O)\,O\,\bm{S}, and the textures of Fig. 1(a) lie in the invariant subspace of this action on bond vectors [21]. In the buckled structure the glide GxG_{x} and the fourfold rotation survive only combined with the horizontal mirror, so they act with the spin rotations C2​xC_{2x} and Rz(−π/2)R_{z}(-\pi/2),

G^x=Gx⊗C2​x,S^4=C4⊗Rz​(−π2),σ^x​y=σx​y⊗C2[1​1¯​0],\hat{G}_{x}=G_{x}\otimes C_{2x},\ \ \hat{S}_{4}=C_{4}\otimes R_{z}(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}),\ \ \hat{\sigma}_{xy}=\sigma_{xy}\otimes C_{2}^{[1\bar{1}0]}, (2)

together with σ^x​y¯\hat{\sigma}_{x\bar{y}} and time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

The low-energy theory is the SU(2) gauge theory of Refs. [11, 50]: eight Majorana-matrix Dirac fields 𝒳\mathcal{X} at the π\pi-flux point, with valley matrices μa\mu^{a} and spin matrices σa\sigma^{a}, coupled to an SU(2) gauge field and to three adjoint Higgs fields Φ1,2,3\Phi_{1,2,3}, of which Φ1\Phi_{1} and Φ2\Phi_{2} are critical at the SO(5) point. Condensing Φ1,Φ2\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2} yields the gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state Z3000, condensing Φ3\Phi_{3} the U(1) state U800 (labels of Ref. [28]). We project the lattice symmetry action, including the projective gauge transformations, onto the Dirac subspace and let each generator act on the spin index through its locked rotation. The Higgs fields are spin singlets, so their potential is unchanged.

No symmetry-allowed gauge-singlet fermion mass at any order in spin–orbit coupling.—The gauge-singlet fermion bilinears Tr⁡[𝒳¯​M​𝒳​σb]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}M\mathcal{X}\sigma^{b}] at zeroth gradient order span a 36-dimensional space. Six are masses [50]: the SO(5) vector Tr⁡[𝒳¯​Γj​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{j}\mathcal{X}], made of the two valence-bond-solid (VBS) components Vx,yV_{x,y} and the three Néel components NaN^{a}, and the flux singlet Tr⁡[𝒳¯​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{X}], which carries the scalar spin chirality χ\chi [54]. The other 30 are components of the conserved SO(5)-adjoint currents. The ten SO(5)-adjoint scalars vanish identically by the Majorana reality condition of the SU(2) theory [21]. Table 1 lists the action of 𝒯\mathcal{T} and G^x\hat{G}_{x} on the six masses. The Néel and chirality masses are odd under time reversal, and the two VBS masses, the only 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even ones, are both odd under the locked glide, so no linear combination is invariant. The locked space group alone suffices: G^x\hat{G}_{x} together with σ^x​y\hat{\sigma}_{xy} leaves no mass invariant, and time reversal is an additional reason for the Néel and chirality masses [1]. Any perturbation that preserves time reversal and the crystal symmetry, DM at any order or the symmetric exchange anisotropies, can therefore generate no gauge-singlet fermion mass. The same holds without spin–orbit coupling, where the unlocked glide plays the role of G^x\hat{G}_{x}. Thus, locking the spins to the lattice allows no new gauge-singlet mass.

Role of the SU(2) gauge structure.—Spin–orbit coupling preserves time reversal and breaks spin rotations, so at linear order it can induce only time-reversal-even operators that carry spin. On kagome one such operator is a mass, the quantum-spin-Hall-type triplet [18]. In the SU(2) gauge theory of the SS spin liquid that whole family, the SO(5)-adjoint scalars, vanishes identically. The 36-dimensional operator space leaves no other candidate. Every time-reversal-even, spin-carrying gauge-singlet bilinear without gradients is a component of a conserved current, and the only spin-carrying masses, the Néel components, are odd under time reversal. The remaining masses are the order parameters of competing states, each of which breaks time reversal or the lattice symmetry, and locking makes none of them symmetric. The two cases thus differ in their gauge group. In the U(1) theory of the kagome Dirac spin liquid the quantum-spin-Hall masses are gauge invariant, whereas in the SU(2) theory of the π\pi-flux state they vanish as gauge singlets. In Z3000 their gauge-adjoint partners reappear, ∝D​⟨Φ⟩\propto D\langle\Phi\rangle, but leave the nodes gapless for material couplings (End Matter).

The theorem concerns explicit local masses in the symmetric state and requires the full layer group. A shear strain along [110][110] lowers it and allows a VBS mass, and a magnetic field allows the masses of Fig. 2. The theorem does not exclude spontaneous symmetry breaking, pairwise annihilation of displaced Dirac nodes of opposite chiral winding (excluded numerically for material couplings in Z3000, End Matter), or confinement by monopoles in the U(1) descendant U800. Its single symmetry-allowed monopole is the SO(5) singlet with or without DM [21].

Linear order and the band touching.—Of the 36 bilinears, DM can induce only those invariant under the symmetries its couplings preserve; they are summarized in Table 2 [21]. With D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} alone the model keeps the spin rotations about cc and the high-temperature symmetries, and no gauge-singlet bilinear without gradients is invariant, even without 𝒯\mathcal{T}. With the in-plane couplings a single bilinear is induced,

δ​ℒ=λ​𝒪DM,𝒪DM=Jxx−Jyy,\delta\mathcal{L}=\lambda\,\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM},\qquad\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM}=J^{x}_{x}-J^{y}_{y}, (3)

where JμaJ^{a}_{\mu} is the current of spin component aa along μ\mu (x|[100]x\parallel[100], y|[010]y\parallel[010]); 𝒪DM\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM} is the spin–orbit-locked component of the SU(2) spin currents allowed by the 4¯​2​m\bar{4}2m point group [Fig. 1(c)]. Time reversal removes two further current combinations. Because JμaJ^{a}_{\mu} are Noether currents of the spin-rotation-invariant fixed point, every component of the current multiplet, and hence 𝒪DM\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM}, has the protected scaling dimension Δ=2\Delta=2 at that fixed point, and λ\lambda has renormalization-group eigenvalue exactly 1. A constant 𝒪DM\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM} is a non-abelian spin vector potential, Ax∝SxA_{x}\propto S^{x}, Ay∝−SyA_{y}\propto-S^{y}. A position-dependent spin rotation maps it at linear order onto spin-dependent node displacements, but because [Ax,Ay]≠0[A_{x},A_{y}]\neq 0 it cannot be removed, and near the critical point, where the Higgs splitting is small, it reconstructs the Dirac nodes below the scale T∗=4​λT^{*}=4\lambda [Fig. 1(e)]. The eightfold node splits into branches at ±4​λ\pm 4\lambda and a dd-wave quadratic band touching, H∝(v2/4​λ)​[(kx2−ky2)​𝒜1+2​kx​ky​𝒜2]H\propto(v^{2}/4\lambda)[(k_{x}^{2}-k_{y}^{2})\mathcal{A}_{1}+2k_{x}k_{y}\mathcal{A}_{2}] with anticommuting matrices 𝒜1,2\mathcal{A}_{1,2}, protected by a chiral symmetry. Projected onto it, the Néel masses Nx,yN^{x,y} vanish and NzN^{z} only splits the bands, whereas Vx,yV_{x,y} and χ\chi open full gaps. Below T∗T^{*}, Néel bilinear order therefore cannot gap the spinons of the band touching. A quadratic band touching is unstable to weak interactions [49, 51]. Here, among gauge-singlet orders, only valence-bond order and a chiral spin liquid can gap it, and a one-loop flow places the instability at T∗⁣∗∼(0.03CLOSET^{**}\sim(0.03–OPEN0.1)​λ0.1)\lambda, in the millikelvin range (End Matter).

A lattice Wick decoupling on the π\pi-flux state estimates the coefficient at mean field, λ=χ0​DΣ′/(2​2)\lambda=\chi_{0}D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}/(2\sqrt{2}), with χ0=0.2395\chi_{0}=0.2395 the nearest-neighbor singlet amplitude and D′Σ=D′∥,s+D′∥,nsD^{\prime}_{\Sigma}=D^{\prime}_{\parallel,s}+D^{\prime}_{\parallel,ns}, 2\sqrt{2} times the in-plane inter-dimer component along the tetragonal axis of each bond, so that T∗≃2​χ0​|DΣ′|≃0.34​|DΣ′|T^{*}\simeq\sqrt{2}\chi_{0}|D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}|\simeq 0.34|D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}| [21]. The intra-dimer D≃0.22D\simeq 0.22–0.350.35 meV [23, 30], the largest DM coupling, does not enter at this order, and D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} cancels. Since DD transforms like the in-plane inter-dimer couplings, it can renormalize λ\lambda beyond mean field, a contribution we do not estimate. Spectroscopy constrains only the combination D∥,s′∓(J′/2J)DD^{\prime}_{\parallel,s}\mp(J^{\prime}/2J)D [5, 41], so DΣ′D^{\prime}_{\Sigma} rests on the one available density-functional calculation [30], which gives T∗≃0.03T^{*}\simeq 0.03–0.170.17 K, uncertainties included (End Matter). The mean-field T∗T^{*} lies below the temperatures of about 1.21.2–1.61.6 K at which the pressurized material orders in zero field [15]. The thermodynamic crossover lies lower still, near (0.1CLOSE(0.1–OPEN0.15)​T∗0.15)T^{*} (End Matter).

The out-of-plane D⟂′≃0.09D^{\prime}_{\perp}\simeq 0.09–0.180.18 meV [4, 41, 30], the largest inter-dimer coupling, enters at linear order only at first gradient order, through the (x​y)(xy) component of a flavored spin-2 current,

OB=Tr⁡[𝒳¯​μy​σz​(γy​i​D↔x+γx​i​D↔y)​𝒳],O_{B}=\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\,\mu^{y}\sigma^{z}(\gamma^{y}\mathrm{i}\overset{\leftrightarrow}{D}_{x}+\gamma^{x}\mathrm{i}\overset{\leftrightarrow}{D}_{y})\mathcal{X}\bigr], (4)

which splits the cone velocities without gapping them [Fig. 1(d)]. A non-conserved spin-2 primary of a unitary conformal field theory has dimension Δ>3\Delta>3 [32, 9], so OBO_{B} is irrelevant at the SO(5) fixed point if that point is unitary; at leading order in 1/N1/N, with N=12N=12, its dimension is 3+16/(5​π2)≃3.323+16/(5\pi^{2})\simeq 3.32 (End Matter).

Second order and SO(5) breaking.—At second order DM induces the rank-2 symmetric tensor of SO(5), the 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14} (𝟓⊗𝟓=𝟏⊕𝟏𝟎⊕𝟏𝟒\mathbf{5}\otimes\mathbf{5}=\mathbf{1}\oplus\mathbf{10}\oplus\mathbf{14}): D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} through OB×OBO_{B}\times O_{B}, since OBO_{B} carries the Néelz flavor μy​σz\mu^{y}\sigma^{z}, and the in-plane couplings at order λ2\lambda^{2}. Its SO(3)×\timesSO(2)-invariant component is the Néel–VBS anisotropy, the tuning operator of the QCD3 and sigma-model descriptions [50, 54, 61]; for it DM only shifts the critical pressure. The rest are spin anisotropies that break the emergent symmetry, easy-axis from D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} and easy-plane from λ\lambda at mean field (End Matter). Whether they matter depends on the dimension of the 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14}, on which the two descriptions of the SO(5) point disagree: it is relevant in the fuzzy-sphere study of the SO(5) sigma model (Δ=1.456\Delta=1.456), obtained there in the walking region [61], and irrelevant at leading order (Δ≃3.46\Delta\simeq 3.46) in the large-NN Higgs theory, tuned instead by the SO(5)-singlet Higgs mass [21]. If the 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14} is irrelevant, no DM-induced SO(5)-breaking four-fermion operator acts above T∗T^{*} within the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) four-fermion spectrum, whose mixing with gauge and Higgs composites outside the 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14} is not computed [21]. If it is relevant, second-order anisotropies do act there, at scales estimated from below 0.10.1 K to about 11 K [21]. In either case the DM-induced Yukawa couplings remain subleading (End Matter). Neither a DM mass nor λ\lambda at linear order can produce the first-order signatures and the bicritical point near 1.31.3 K [15]. They may instead come from a second-order anisotropy, the interlayer coupling or disorder [21].

Field selection rule.—A magnetic field lowers the symmetry to the stabilizer of (DM,𝑩)(\text{DM},\bm{B}): the locked elements that fix 𝑩\bm{B} and the products of 𝒯\mathcal{T} with those that reverse it. Classifying the 36 bilinears under these groups gives the activated masses of Fig. 2 [21]. For 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] the only activated mass is the flux singlet, so the field couples linearly to the scalar chirality. For the Zeeman coupling this requires spin–orbit locking, because without it the magnetization is a spin triplet and χ\chi a singlet. No Néel component is allowed at any order in BB. For an in-plane field the Néel moment is activated at linear order with the tensor Nx∝ByN^{x}\propto B_{y}, Ny∝BxN^{y}\propto B_{x}. Up to a non-universal sign, 𝑵\bm{N} is the mirror image of 𝑩\bm{B} in the [110][110] dimer axis, perpendicular to 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] and on the axis of 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110]. The order in the DM couplings follows from the horizontal mirror σ^h\hat{\sigma}_{h}, which acts on the spins as a global C2​zC_{2z} rotation. It maps the model onto itself with every in-plane DM component and the in-plane components of 𝑩\bm{B} and 𝑵\bm{N} reversed, so the in-plane Néel response to an in-plane field is even in the in-plane DM couplings and absent at first order. The intra-dimer DD alone already produces it at second order, and D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} alone, which conserves SzS^{z}, gives none at any order. A dependence of the in-plane gg tensor on the dimer orientation, allowed by the Cu site symmetry, enters at first order in spin–orbit coupling. With components g1g_{1} along the dimer and g2g_{2} across it, the Zeeman term contains the staggered field 12​(g1−g2)​μB​∑iϵi​(By​Six+Bx​Siy)\tfrac{1}{2}(g_{1}-g_{2})\mu_{B}\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}(B_{y}S_{i}^{x}+B_{x}S_{i}^{y}) with the same tensor, which together with DM produces the field-induced gap in Cu benzoate [38]. It induces a moment wherever the staggered susceptibility ∂⟨𝑵⟩/∂hs\partial\langle\bm{N}\rangle/\partial h_{s} is finite, which excludes only the exact dimer singlet at zero temperature. The two inversion twins of the crystal [48] carry opposite in-plane DM, so the even response has the same sign in both.

Because the rule rests only on the lattice symmetry, it also holds in the dimer phase, where it is distinct from the first-order intra-dimer staggered moments of Refs. [23, 34, 33], which are antiparallel within each dimer and lie along cc for an in-plane field. The rule predicts that a 11B NMR comparison of 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] with 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001] at matched Zeeman energy under pressure and below HcH_{c}, above the plaquette ordering temperature, shows a Néel-pattern splitting, with the moments of each dimer parallel, only for the in-plane field, provided the moment transfers a hyperfine field to the boron site. Because a cc-axis field also splits the lines, through the intra-dimer staggered moments, the two field directions are distinguished by the pattern of the splitting. No experiment has made this comparison (End Matter). In the spin-liquid regime the [100][100] moment grows toward the critical pressure as ms∝B​ξ3−2​ΔNm_{s}\propto B\,\xi^{3-2\Delta_{N}} (ξ\xi the correlation length, ΔN\Delta_{N} the Néel dimension), with exponent 0.080.08 at leading order in 1/N1/N, small enough for a regular background to dominate, and of order one for ΔN≃0.63\Delta_{N}\simeq 0.63 [37]. For field-tuned tests of deconfined criticality, any in-plane component of the field, as in a tilted field, is linearly conjugate to the in-plane Néel order parameter [Fig. 2(e)] and rounds a critical point on a scale of 0.10.1–11 K for the 8.6∘8.6^{\circ} tilt of Ref. [8] and an illustrative gg anisotropy (End Matter).

Outlook.—The spin–orbit coupling of SrCu2(BO3)2 cannot give its Dirac spinons a gauge-singlet mass. At linear order it only twists the spinons through a conserved current, which below T∗T^{*} reconstructs the nodes into a band touching that, among gauge-singlet orders, is open to valence-bond and chiral order but not to Néel order. Above T∗T^{*} it can act, apart from Yukawa couplings that start below 2%2\% of the one that bounds the pseudocritical window, only through second-order rank-2 anisotropies. Their relevance, fixed by the dimension of the SO(5) 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14}, and the signs and sizes of their DM-seeded coefficients remain open. The no-mass theorem uses only the time-reversal oddness of the Néel and chirality masses, the lattice parities of the spin-singlet VBS masses, which locking cannot change, and the absence of quantum-spin-Hall masses in the SU(2) theory. It therefore carries over to any lattice realization of this gauge theory whose SO(5) vector consists of Néel and VBS order parameters and whose crystal symmetry leaves no VBS combination invariant.

End Matter

Continuum theory and locked action.—Projecting the lattice projective symmetry group of Ref. [11] onto the node subspace, with each generator carrying its axial spin rotation, gives the continuum action of the locked generators of Eq. (2) and σ^x​y¯=σx​y¯⊗C2[110]\hat{\sigma}_{x\bar{y}}=\sigma_{x\bar{y}}\otimes C_{2}^{[110]} (Supplemental Material [1]). The emergent SO(5) has generators Tj={μy,σa,μx​σa,μz​σa}T^{j}=\{\mu^{y},\sigma^{a},\mu^{x}\sigma^{a},\mu^{z}\sigma^{a}\} and vector Γj={μx,μz,μy​σa}\Gamma^{j}=\{\mu^{x},\mu^{z},\mu^{y}\sigma^{a}\}, with Dirac matrices γ0=ρy\gamma^{0}=\rho^{y}, γx=i​ρz\gamma^{x}=\mathrm{i}\rho^{z}, γy=i​ρx\gamma^{y}=\mathrm{i}\rho^{x}.

The gauge-singlet bilinears.—The Hermitian gauge-singlet bilinears at zeroth gradient order form the gauge-invariant subspace of the 120 quadratic Majorana forms, of dimension 36: the six masses and the 30 components of the currents Tr⁡[𝒳¯​γμ​Tj​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\gamma^{\mu}T^{j}\mathcal{X}]. The ten scalars Tr⁡[𝒳¯​Tj​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}T^{j}\mathcal{X}] vanish identically, because the reality condition makes each of them the trace of a product that changes sign under transposition [21]. The tables of all 36 operators under the unlocked, buckled-locked and high-temperature-locked generators are given in the Supplemental Material [1]. The gauge-adjoint bilinears transform as in Ref. [11]. Reference [50] agrees except for the time-reversal signs of the Néel-flavored currents Tr⁡[σa​𝒳¯​μy​σb​γμ​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\sigma^{a}\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mu^{y}\sigma^{b}\gamma^{\mu}\mathcal{X}], which the time-reversal oddness of the Néel mass fixes as in Ref. [11] (Supplemental Material [1]). The no-mass theorem uses only two columns of these tables (Table 1). The tabulated spin labels, related to physical axes by x→−xx\to-x, leave these columns unchanged and turn Eq. (3) into Tr⁡[𝒳¯​γx​𝒳​σx]+Tr⁡[𝒳¯​γy​𝒳​σy]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\gamma^{x}\mathcal{X}\sigma^{x}]+\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\gamma^{y}\mathcal{X}\sigma^{y}]. A construction directly in physical axes gives the same classification and invariant Jxx−JyyJ^{x}_{x}-J^{y}_{y} [1].

At the critical point and in the Higgs phases the gauge-adjoint bilinears enter through Yukawa couplings. With D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} no new Yukawa coupling is allowed. With the in-plane components three appear, including the first zeroth-order coupling of Φ3\Phi_{3} [21]. At the multicritical point the first two are relevant: one is an SO(5) and Lorentz partner of the Yukawa coupling yy of Ref. [11], the other, a scalar, is less relevant than yy at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N). Only the intra-dimer DD generates them, starting at 6×10−46\times 10^{-4}–2×10−22\times 10^{-2} of yy barring a cancellation among the Z3000 amplitudes, so they remain subleading throughout the pseudocritical window [21]. In Z3000 they become quadratic terms proportional to D​⟨Φ⟩D\langle\Phi\rangle, which the singlet argument does not control. There the nodes are protected by a chiral symmetry: the Bogoliubov Hamiltonian with every DM term anticommutes with (−1)ix+iy(-1)^{i_{x}+i_{y}} times an on-site rotation, so each node carries a winding number, and a direct diagonalization finds the nodes gapless up to couplings far beyond the material values [21]. In the U(1) state U800 the locked group admits a zeroth-order Φ3\Phi_{3} coupling only to a current but none to a mass [21]. Non-magnetic quenched disorder couples a relevant random field to the valence-bond doublet and none to the chirality or Néel channels [21].

The coefficient λ\lambda.—The Wick decoupling of 𝑫⋅(𝑺i×𝑺j)\bm{D}\cdot(\bm{S}_{i}\times\bm{S}_{j}) in the singlet channel ⟨fi​α†​fj​β⟩=χi​j​δα​β\langle f^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}f_{j\beta}\rangle=\chi_{ij}\delta_{\alpha\beta} gives the triplet hopping i2𝑫⋅(χi​jfj†𝝈fi−h.c.)\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\bm{D}\cdot(\chi_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{j}\bm{\sigma}f_{i}-{\rm h.c.}). On the π\pi-flux state (|χi​j|=χ0=0.23952|\chi_{ij}|=\chi_{0}=0.23952 in the thermodynamic limit) the sum over the eight inter-dimer bonds of a cell projects onto pure 𝒪DM\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM} with λ=χ0​DΣ′/(2​2)\lambda=\chi_{0}D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}/(2\sqrt{2}); D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} cancels, and the intra-dimer DD drops out because the dimer amplitude vanishes on the π\pi-flux state. At linear order the DM term acts as a background spin gauge field. It twists the spinon hopping by an angle of order DΣ′/J′D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}/J^{\prime}, so the node splitting scales with the spinon velocity. The Fock value above and a hopping t≃0.4​J′t\simeq 0.4J^{\prime} therefore give splittings that differ by a factor of 1.71.7, which sets the uncertainty of the mean-field prefactor. The specific heat of the free spinons crosses over to the band-touching regime only near (0.1CLOSE(0.1–OPEN0.15)​T∗0.15)T^{*}, because the reconstructed band is quadratic only well below λ\lambda [21].

Triplon spectroscopy fixes D∥,s′∓(J′/2J)D≃0.07D^{\prime}_{\parallel,s}\mp(J^{\prime}/2J)D\simeq 0.07–0.080.08 meV [5, 41] and is blind to D′∥,nsD^{\prime}_{\parallel,ns} at linear order. The only tabulated inter-dimer DM vectors [30], placed on their bonds with the bond vectors of that calculation [31], give D⟂′≃−0.10D^{\prime}_{\perp}\simeq-0.10 meV and an in-plane component of 0.010.01 meV along the tetragonal axis of each bond. This yields |DΣ′|≃0.014|D^{\prime}_{\Sigma}|\simeq 0.014 meV, or 0.0070.007–0.0250.025 meV once the rounding of the table and a rescaling to the electron-spin-resonance value of D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} are included, and hence T∗≃0.03T^{*}\simeq 0.03–0.10.1 K at the Fock level, rising to 0.170.17 K for t≃0.4​J′t\simeq 0.4J^{\prime}. These are ambient-pressure couplings; the buckling that allows the in-plane components may decrease under pressure [27], which would lower T∗T^{*}.

The band touching below T∗T^{*}.—At the node the Dirac Hamiltonian is h⁡(𝒌)=v⁡(kx​ρx−ky​ρz)+λ​hDMh(\bm{k})=v(k_{x}\rho^{x}-k_{y}\rho^{z})+\lambda h_{\rm DM}, where hDMh_{\rm DM} is the single-particle matrix that 𝒪DM\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM} adds at 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0. It splits the eightfold multiplet into branches at ±4​λ\pm 4\lambda and four gapless modes. Second-order k⋅pk\cdot p theory gives HQBT=(v2/4​λ)​[(kx2−ky2)​𝒜1+2​kx​ky​𝒜2]H_{\rm QBT}=(v^{2}/4\lambda)[(k_{x}^{2}-k_{y}^{2})\mathcal{A}_{1}+2k_{x}k_{y}\mathcal{A}_{2}] with {𝒜1,𝒜2}=0\{\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2}\}=0, Berry winding 2, isotropic at all kk. A k2​𝟙k^{2}\mathds{1} term is forbidden by the chiral symmetry ρy\rho^{y}, which anticommutes with h⁡(𝒌)h(\bm{k}) including the DM term. On the band-touching subspace, NxN^{x} and NyN^{y} vanish because they live on the ±4​λ\pm 4\lambda branches, NzN^{z} commutes with 𝒜1,2\mathcal{A}_{1,2} and splits the bands into pockets, and VxV_{x}, VyV_{y} and the flux singlet anticommute with both and open full gaps. On this subspace the uniform magnetization obeys P⁡(J0​σz)=−P⁡(flux)P(J^{0}\sigma^{z})=-P(\text{flux}), so the chirality carries a weak zz moment and a cc-axis field couples to it linearly. A one-loop flow of the 14 locked-invariant quartic couplings with the screened gauge field ends on a valence-bond ray for the material’s exchange, and otherwise on a gapped chiral ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid, at T∗⁣∗∼(0.03CLOSET^{**}\sim(0.03–OPEN0.1)​λ0.1)\lambda. This regime requires a two-dimensional sample and a pseudocritical window that reaches T∗T^{*} [21].

The spin-2 operator and the second-order tensor.—Being flavored, OBO_{B} cannot mix with gauge or Higgs operators at y=0y=0. At O⁡(1/N)O(1/N), with N=2​Nf+4​Nb=12N=2N_{f}+4N_{b}=12 the gauge-polarization count of two Dirac valleys and two real adjoint Higgs triplets, the self-energy, vertex and the two seagull graphs of the covariant derivative give γ2=64​Cg/(5​π2​N)=16/(5​π2)≃0.32\gamma_{2}=64C_{g}/(5\pi^{2}N)=16/(5\pi^{2})\simeq 0.32 at Casimir Cg=3C_{g}=3, independent of the gauge parameter. At Cg=1C_{g}=1 this reduces to the QED3 flavor-adjoint spin-2 anomalous dimension of Ref. [60], with CgC_{g} placed as in Ref. [13]. The same rules give the valence-bond and Néel dimension ΔN=2−64​Cg/(3​π2​N)≃1.46\Delta_{N}=2-64C_{g}/(3\pi^{2}N)\simeq 1.46 (QED3 adjoint value [40, 19] at Cg=1C_{g}=1) and, at the y=0y=0 large-NN Higgs fixed point, the scalar four-fermion operator in the SO(5) 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14} forms an isolated irrep with Δ𝟏𝟒=4−64/(π2​N)≃3.46\Delta_{\mathbf{14}}=4-64/(\pi^{2}N)\simeq 3.46 for N=12N=12 at this order. With 64/π2​N≃0.5464/\pi^{2}N\simeq 0.54 these values fix only signs and orderings, and whether the 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14} is relevant is open. The Higgs sector is less controlled: its constraint field has Δσ=0.38\Delta_{\sigma}=0.38 at O⁡(1/N)O(1/N), below the unitarity bound 1/21/2, so SO(5)-singlet dimensions at N=12N=12 are not controlled [21]. The bound Δ>3\Delta>3 for OBO_{B} does not rest on the expansion; it assumes a unitary critical point and does not apply in the walking scenario with complex fixed points [54]. The seagull sign is fixed by gauge covariance, and the same rules give the full spin-ℓ\ell tower [21].

At second order, a Kubo computation of the mass-channel responses with the Wick-decoupled D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} operator gives rank-2 coefficients τ1=−0.18\tau_{1}=-0.18 and τ2=−1.94\tau_{2}=-1.94 per (D⟂′/t)2(D^{\prime}_{\perp}/t)^{2}, in the channel basis τ1​diag​(3,3,−2,−2,−2)+τ2​diag​(0,0,1,1,−2)\tau_{1}\,{\rm diag}(3,3,-2,-2,-2)+\tau_{2}\,{\rm diag}(0,0,1,1,-2) on (Vx,Vy,Nx,Ny,Nz)(V_{x},V_{y},N^{x},N^{y},N^{z}), nearly temperature independent and dominated by the lattice scale. They describe an easy-axis anisotropy (τ2<0\tau_{2}<0) with a Néel-side tuning component (τ1<0\tau_{1}<0) [21]. The normalization is arbitrary, so only signs and ratios are meaningful. The in-plane couplings give τ1,τ2>0\tau_{1},\tau_{2}>0 of order λ2/T\lambda^{2}/T, an easy-plane anisotropy with a singlet-side tuning component. The D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} term dominates above T×≃0.01T_{\times}\simeq 0.01–0.30.3 K at the Fock level [21]. The coefficients grow with the momentum cutoff, so the sign is a lattice-scale, mean-field result; a classical bond-level estimate of the same order, D⟂′2/2​J′2D^{\prime 2}_{\perp}/2J^{\prime 2}, is easy-plane instead. The intra-dimer DD, which has no mean-field image, the symmetric exchange anisotropies and the dipolar coupling generate the same tensor at the same order and are not computed. For a single bond, DM and the symmetric anisotropy of the same order are equivalent to isotropic exchange by a local spin rotation [46]. If the 𝟏𝟒\mathbf{14} is relevant with yT=3−1.456≃1.54y_{T}=3-1.456\simeq 1.54, a coupling gTg_{T} becomes of order one at ET≃Λ​gT1/yTE_{T}\simeq\Lambda g_{T}^{1/y_{T}}, with Λ≃t\Lambda\simeq t the lattice cutoff. The mean-field coefficient gives ET≃0.03E_{T}\simeq 0.03–0.070.07 K, a coefficient of the bond-level size 0.10.1–0.20.2 K (0.20.2–0.50.5 K with Λ=J′\Lambda=J^{\prime}), and one of order one 0.50.5–11 K.

The field selection rule.—The stabilizer of (DM,𝑩)(\text{DM},\bm{B}) contains the locked elements OO with O​𝑩=𝑩O\bm{B}=\bm{B} and the products 𝒯​O\mathcal{T}O with O​𝑩=−𝑩O\bm{B}=-\bm{B}. Classifying the 36 bilinears under it gives, for 𝑩|[001]\bm{B}\parallel[001], only the flux singlet; for 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] the Néel component NyN^{y}; for 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110] the component (Nx+Ny)/2(N^{x}+N^{y})/\sqrt{2} and, at order Bx​ByB_{x}B_{y}, the valence-bond imbalance Vx−VyV_{x}-V_{y}. The order in the DM couplings follows from σ^h\hat{\sigma}_{h}, which maps H⁡(𝑫∥,D⟂′,𝑩)H(\bm{D}_{\parallel},D^{\prime}_{\perp},\bm{B}) onto H⁡(−𝑫∥,D⟂′,C2​z​𝑩)H(-\bm{D}_{\parallel},D^{\prime}_{\perp},C_{2z}\bm{B}) and reverses Nx,yN^{x,y}; the locked group of the high-temperature structure, which contains σ^h\hat{\sigma}_{h} and therefore classifies the even orders, still allows the tensor (Nx,Ny)∝(By,Bx)(N^{x},N^{y})\propto(B_{y},B_{x}). A Gaussian computation on the π\pi-flux state with the Wick-decoupled DM operator confirms the rule: the Néel source is linear in BB and proportional to λD′∥,s\lambda D^{\prime}_{\parallel,s}, of second order in the in-plane couplings, along [010][010] for 𝑩|[100]\bm{B}\parallel[100] and along [110][110] for 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110].

Exact diagonalization of Eq. (1) with the DM vectors of the I​4¯​2​mI\bar{4}2m structure confirms the rule independently of the gauge theory, on a 16-site cluster that keeps the full buckled group, a 20-site cluster that keeps S^4\hat{S}_{4}, and an 8-site cluster at finite temperature. On the 16-site cluster the linear response of 𝑵\bm{N} to 𝑩\bm{B} is the pure off-diagonal tensor (Nx,Ny)∝(By,Bx)(N^{x},N^{y})\propto(B_{y},B_{x}), and every other entry is below 10−1510^{-15}; it is even under 𝑫∥→−𝑫∥\bm{D}_{\parallel}\to-\bm{D}_{\parallel} to 2×10−142\times 10^{-14} and quadratic in the in-plane couplings; D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} alone gives no response, and 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c induces no Néel moment up to B=0.3​JB=0.3J. Its sign changes with J′/JJ^{\prime}/J and with temperature. A cc-axis field induces only the intra-dimer staggered moments of Ref. [23], and with a dimer-dependent gg tensor and no DM the Néel response equals 12​(g1−g2)​∂⟨𝑵⟩/∂hs\tfrac{1}{2}(g_{1}-g_{2})\,\partial\langle\bm{N}\rangle/\partial h_{s}.

No experiment has compared [100][100] with cc: Refs. [8, 7] applied the field along cc or 8.6∘8.6^{\circ} from it, in an uncharacterized in-plane direction, and Ref. [53] compared 𝑩|c\bm{B}\parallel c with 𝑩|[110]\bm{B}\parallel[110] at 2.42.4 GPa at equal field. At 2.42.4 GPa and 88 T along [100][100], above HcH_{c}, Ref. [55] resolved no line splitting down to 1.81.8 K, which bounds the [100][100] response but does not test its orientation dependence. The plaquette order (TP≃1.6T_{P}\simeq 1.6 K at 2.42.4 GPa and 44 T [7]) lowers the layer symmetry, so the comparison belongs above TPT_{P}. For a tilted field the conjugate staggered field is hs∼12​(g1−g2)​μB​B​sin⁡θh_{s}\sim\tfrac{1}{2}(g_{1}-g_{2})\mu_{B}B\sin\theta plus a term of second order in the in-plane DM couplings. It is relevant with eigenvalue 3−ΔN3-\Delta_{N} and rounds a critical point on the scale Th∼Λ​(hs/Λ)1/(3−ΔN)T_{h}\sim\Lambda(h_{s}/\Lambda)^{1/(3-\Delta_{N})}. For an illustrative |g1−g2|=10−2|g_{1}-g_{2}|=10^{-2}, the 8.6∘8.6^{\circ} tilt of Ref. [8] at Hc≃5.7H_{c}\simeq 5.7 T and a cutoff Λ≃J′\Lambda\simeq J^{\prime}–J≃50J\simeq 50–8585 K give Th∼0.1T_{h}\sim 0.1 K at ΔN=1.46\Delta_{N}=1.46 and ∼1\sim 1 K at ΔN≃0.63\Delta_{N}\simeq 0.63.

Supplemental Material

This Supplemental Material lists the transformation tables on which the no-mass theorem and the operator selection of the Letter rest, and the bond-resolved Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) textures. Derivations and all further details, including the one-loop and O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) results quoted in the Letter, are given in the companion paper [21]. Rows are labeled by the matrix M​σbM\sigma^{b} of the gauge-singlet bilinear Tr⁡[𝒳¯​M​𝒳​σb]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}M\mathcal{X}\sigma^{b}] (notation of the Letter); the entries give the image under each generator (±\pm alone means ±\pm the same row). The tables use spin labels related to physical axes by x→−xx\to-x; this relabeling does not change any sign on the diagonal.

Continuum theory and locked action

The Majorana-matrix formulation [50, 11] combines the spinons into ℱi=(fi↑−fi↓fi↓†fi↑†)\mathcal{F}_{i}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}f_{i\uparrow}&-f_{i\downarrow}\\ f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}&f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) with ℱi†=σy​ℱiT​σy\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\dagger}=\sigma^{y}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{T}\sigma^{y}. SU(2) gauge transformations act on the left and spin rotations Ω\Omega on the right, ℱ→ℱ​σz​ΩT​σz\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}\sigma^{z}\Omega^{T}\sigma^{z}. Near the π\pi-flux nodes the field 𝒳\mathcal{X} carries Dirac (γ0=ρy\gamma^{0}=\rho^{y}, γx=i​ρz\gamma^{x}=\mathrm{i}\rho^{z}, γy=i​ρx\gamma^{y}=\mathrm{i}\rho^{x}), valley (μa\mu^{a}), spin and gauge indices, 𝒳¯=𝒳†​γ0\bar{\mathcal{X}}=\mathcal{X}^{\dagger}\gamma^{0}, and the emergent SO(5) has generators Tj={μy,σa,μx​σa,μz​σa}T^{j}=\{\mu^{y},\sigma^{a},\mu^{x}\sigma^{a},\mu^{z}\sigma^{a}\} and vector Γj={μx,μz,μy​σa}\Gamma^{j}=\{\mu^{x},\mu^{z},\mu^{y}\sigma^{a}\}. Projecting the lattice projective symmetry group of Ref. [11] onto the node subspace gives Gx:𝒳→ρx​𝒳​(x,−y)G_{x}:\mathcal{X}\to\rho^{x}\mathcal{X}(x,-y), 𝒯:𝒳→ρy​μy​𝒳\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{X}\to\rho^{y}\mu^{y}\mathcal{X} with i→−i\mathrm{i}\to-\mathrm{i} and an additional i​σy\mathrm{i}\sigma^{y} on the spin index, and σx​y:𝒳→−ρzμze−iπρy/4ei​π​μy/4𝒳(y,x)\sigma_{xy}:\mathcal{X}\to-\rho^{z}\mu^{z}e^{-\mathrm{i}\pi\rho^{y}/4}e^{\mathrm{i}\pi\mu^{y}/4}\mathcal{X}(y,x). With DM each generator carries its axial spin rotation as the right factor σz​ΩOT​σz\sigma^{z}\Omega_{O}^{T}\sigma^{z}: Eq. (2) of the Letter and σ^x​y¯=σx​y¯⊗C2[110]\hat{\sigma}_{x\bar{y}}=\sigma_{x\bar{y}}\otimes C_{2}^{[110]} for the buckled structure. The high-temperature structure adds the mirror σ^h=𝟙⊗C2​z\hat{\sigma}_{h}=\mathds{1}\otimes C_{2z}, the pure glide Gx⊗C2​yG_{x}\otimes C_{2y} and the pure rotation C4⊗Rz(+π/2)C_{4}\otimes R_{z}(+\pi/2), and with D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} alone the full spin U(1)z. The Higgs fields transform as in the unlocked theory.

Independent construction in physical axes

The classification is corroborated by an independent construction of the continuum symmetry action and of the 36 gauge-singlet bilinears directly in physical axes (x|[100]x\parallel[100], y|[010]y\parallel[010]). It yields the same inventory of six masses and 30 conserved-current components, the vanishing of the ten SO(5)-adjoint scalars, and Table S2 under the identification σlabelx=−Sx\sigma^{x}_{\rm label}=-S^{x}. The single invariant under the buckled locked group with 𝒯\mathcal{T} is Jxx−JyyJ^{x}_{x}-J^{y}_{y}, the Dresselhaus form of 4¯​2​m\bar{4}2m. The bond-resolved DM textures of Table S4 project onto it alone, and D⟂′D^{\prime}_{\perp} projects to zero. The locked space group alone forbids all six masses; the pairs {G^x,σ^x​y}\{\hat{G}_{x},\hat{\sigma}_{xy}\}, {G^x,σ^x​y¯}\{\hat{G}_{x},\hat{\sigma}_{x\bar{y}}\}, {G^x,S^4}\{\hat{G}_{x},\hat{S}_{4}\}, {σ^x​y,S^4}\{\hat{\sigma}_{xy},\hat{S}_{4}\} and {σ^x​y¯,S^4}\{\hat{\sigma}_{x\bar{y}},\hat{S}_{4}\} each suffice, whereas time reversal together with translations leaves both VBS masses allowed.

Comparison with published gauge-adjoint tables

Under the continuum symmetry action of Tables S1–S3, the transformations of the gauge-adjoint bilinears Tr⁡[σa​𝒳¯​M​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\sigma^{a}\bar{\mathcal{X}}M\mathcal{X}] agree entry by entry with Tables 2 and 3 of Ref. [11] (GxG_{x}, 𝒯\mathcal{T}, σx​y\sigma_{xy}; Pauli matrices written there as τ\tau) and with Figs. 3 and 4 of Ref. [50] (𝒯\mathcal{T}, PxP_{x}, PyP_{y}, TxT_{x}, TyT_{y}, Rπ/2R_{\pi/2}; the Rπ/2R_{\pi/2} images agree up to the sign convention of the representatives within each two-cycle), with one exception. For the Néel-flavored currents Tr⁡[σa​𝒳¯​μy​σb​γμ​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\sigma^{a}\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mu^{y}\sigma^{b}\gamma^{\mu}\mathcal{X}], μ=0,x,y\mu=0,x,y, Ref. [50] lists the time-reversal parities (+,−,−)(+,-,-), whereas the present construction and Ref. [11] give (−,+,+)(-,+,+).

The parities (−,+,+)(-,+,+) follow from two facts. Each of these bilinears is Hermitian as written, because its kernel is a product of Hermitian Pauli matrices, so no factor of i\mathrm{i} enters. The antiunitary 𝒯\mathcal{T} acts on a kernel AA as A→W†​A∗​WA\to W^{\dagger}A^{*}W, a multiplicative map, and the Dirac, valley, spin and gauge matrices act on different tensor factors. The Néel-flavored and valence-bond-flavored currents with the same gauge and Dirac factors therefore differ in time-reversal parity by the same factor as the Néel mass Tr⁡[𝒳¯​μy​𝒳​σb]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mu^{y}\mathcal{X}\sigma^{b}] and the valence-bond masses Tr⁡[𝒳¯​μx,z​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\mu^{x,z}\mathcal{X}], which is −1-1: the Néel order parameter is odd under time reversal and the valence-bond one even (Table S1). Given the published parities (+,−,−)(+,-,-) of the μx​γμ\mu^{x}\gamma^{\mu} and μz​γμ\mu^{z}\gamma^{\mu} rows, the μy​σb​γμ\mu^{y}\sigma^{b}\gamma^{\mu} rows must be (−,+,+)(-,+,+). The same conclusion follows within Ref. [50] from its own table of Tr⁡[σa​𝒳¯​Tj​𝒳]\mathrm{Tr}[\sigma^{a}\bar{\mathcal{X}}T^{j}\mathcal{X}], whose time-reversal column agrees with the present construction. The discrepancy leaves the gauge-singlet classification of the Letter unchanged. It enters only the Yukawa couplings of the companion paper that contain these currents, for which the parities (−,+,+)(-,+,+) are used [21].
